posts.title: FireClient 1.1: Device Scaling, Pro Crash Reporter and License Page
posts.excerpt: Adaptive screen scaling from compact laptops to 4K monitors, a built-in Pro Crash Reporter with 1-click auto-fix, Potato PC booster, and a published license and safety facts page.
posts.body:
FireClient 1.1 is now available. This update focuses on stability, universal screen resolution support, seamless offline gameplay, and a published license and safety facts page.

## What is new in FireClient 1.1

### 1. Universal Screen Scaling & Device Support
Whether you are playing on a 1366x768 / 1280x720 laptop screen, a 1080p desktop, or a 4K high-DPI gaming display, FireClient 1.1 automatically scales its interface:
- Dynamic Per-Monitor V2 DPI awareness prevents blurry text and oversized windows.
- Adaptive layout constraints ensure buttons, version pickers, and sidebar navigation never clip or overflow on small displays.
- High-resolution asset rendering for sharp visuals on 1440p and 4K displays.

### 2. Pro Crash Reporter & 1-Click Auto-Fix
When Minecraft or a mod encounters an error, FireClient now presents a dedicated Crash Dialog instead of an unexpected exit:
- Automatic root cause diagnostics parsing crash reports and logs.
- Identifies mismatched mod builds, outdated OpenGL drivers, or insufficient memory.
- **1-Click Auto-Fix & Restart:** Quarantines conflicting mods and applies safe graphics defaults to get you back in game immediately.
- Real-time hardware summary showing active CPU, GPU, and system RAM.

### 3. Potato PC & Hardware Optimizer
Integrated performance optimizations for Intel HD/UHD and AMD Radeon processors:
- Fast graphics profiles and optimized render distances for budget laptops.
- Smart JVM garbage collection flags (-XX:+UseG1GC) for stutter-free gameplay.
- Tailored OpenGL workarounds for legacy integrated graphics chips.

### 4. Offline Mode Without WiFi
FireClient now fully supports launching guest and offline profiles without an internet connection. Play offline anywhere with zero network timeouts.

### 5. License and safety facts
We have published a plain-language [license and safety facts page](/license.html). It makes no guarantees and does not claim an independent audit:
- The installer is still unsigned, so Windows may warn about it. Check the SHA-256 on the [download page](/download/) when one is shown.
- Microsoft sign-in tokens are stored encrypted with Windows DPAPI under your Windows user account, according to the maintainers.
- The maintainers state that FireClient does not send your tokens or passwords to any FireClient server.

## Getting the update

Existing users can download the update from the [Download page](https://www.fireclient.net/download/) or GitHub Releases. Read the [license and safety facts](/license.html) or join our [Discord](https://discord.gg/r23YNWWfrx) for help.

posts.author: FirePDX
posts.title: How to switch or downgrade Minecraft versions safely
posts.metaTitle: Switch or Downgrade Minecraft Versions Safely
posts.metaDescription: Switch Minecraft versions without losing worlds: back up first, use separate profiles, never open a newer world in an older version, and keep mods matched.
posts.excerpt: Use separate profiles, back up first and avoid the one mistake that can ruin a world when going back to an older version.
posts.body:
You may want an older version for a server, a mod or a favourite world. Going forward is usually fine. Going back is where worlds get damaged, so follow these steps.

## The one rule

**Do not open a world in an older version than the one that last saved it.** Newer versions change how worlds are stored, and an older version may fail to load it or corrupt it. Minecraft shows a warning in many cases, so read it and back out.

## 1. Back up first

Close the game and [back up your worlds](/blog/backup-minecraft-worlds-windows/). Copy the world folder somewhere safe before you try any version change.

## 2. Use a separate profile

Create a new profile for the version you want, instead of changing your main one. In the [FireClient launcher](/download/) the Minecraft version and loader are set per profile, so keep one profile per version and loader.

## 3. Match Java to the version

Different Minecraft versions need different Java versions. Minecraft 1.21.1 needs Java 21. Older versions may need an older Java. Check with the [Java version checker](/tools/minecraft-java-version-checker/) and the [Java 21 guide](/blog/install-java-21-for-minecraft-1-21-1/).

## 4. Match your mods

Mods are built for one Minecraft version and one loader. When you switch versions, install the versions of the mods that match. See the [mods guide](/blog/install-fabric-mods-modrinth-minecraft-1-21-1/) and the [loader comparison](/blog/fabric-vs-forge-vs-neoforge-vs-quilt/).

## 5. Test with a copy

Make a copy of the world, put the copy in the older version's saves folder and try it there. Keep the original untouched.

## Updating to a newer version

Back up, make a new profile for the new version and open a copy of your world first. Check that your mods have updated before you move your main profile.

## If something breaks

Restore your backup and use the [crash checklist](/blog/fix-minecraft-crash-fabric-1-21-1/). Ask in the [FireClient Discord](https://discord.gg/r23YNWWfrx) and never post account files or tokens.

posts.title: How to change your Minecraft skin (Java Edition)
posts.metaTitle: How to Change Your Minecraft Skin on Java Edition
posts.metaDescription: Change your Minecraft Java skin: upload a PNG to your account, pick classic or slim, see it in game, and what local skins in a launcher can and cannot do.
posts.excerpt: Upload a skin to your account, choose the model and fix the common problems, plus how local skins differ.
posts.body:
Your skin is stored on your Minecraft account, so other players see it on servers. Here is how to change it on Java Edition, and how local skins in a launcher differ.

## Change the skin on your account

1. Sign in at minecraft.net with the Microsoft account that owns Minecraft Java Edition.
2. Open your profile and find the skin section.
3. Upload a skin file. It must be a PNG, normally 64 by 64 pixels.
4. Choose the arm model, **classic** (wider arms) or **slim** (narrower arms), to match your skin.
5. Save, then restart the game or rejoin the server.

## If the skin does not change

- Wait a minute and restart the game, because servers and caches update slowly
- Check that you signed in with the right account, see the [sign-in guide](/blog/fix-minecraft-microsoft-sign-in-error/)
- Check the file is a valid PNG and not a renamed image
- Try the other arm model if the arms look wrong

## Local skins in a launcher

A launcher can also keep skins on your PC. FireClient lists local skins among its features, and they are stored on your computer. A local skin is only for you, so other players on a server will not see it. To change what others see, change the skin on your account.

## Where to get skins

Make your own with a skin editor, or use skins from sites whose terms allow it. Only download image files (.png) and never run an .exe that claims to be a skin, as explained in the [safe mods checklist](/blog/how-to-find-safe-minecraft-mods/).

## Keep your account safe

Never share your password or access tokens with a site that offers to apply a skin for you. Upload skins only on minecraft.net or in a launcher you trust.

posts.title: How to run Minecraft smoothly on a laptop (Windows 10 and 11)
posts.metaTitle: Run Minecraft Smoothly on a Laptop: Windows 10 and 11
posts.metaDescription: Improve Minecraft on a laptop: plug in, pick the right graphics chip, use a high-performance power plan, lower distances and keep it cool.
posts.excerpt: Power, graphics chip, settings and cooling: the laptop-specific steps that raise Minecraft frame rates.
posts.body:
Laptops lose frame rate for reasons desktops do not: battery saving, switching graphics chips and heat. These steps fix the most common ones for Minecraft Java Edition on Windows 10 and 11.

## 1. Plug in

Many laptops slow down on battery. Plug in the charger before you play.

## 2. Use a high-performance power mode

Open Windows Settings, System, Power (or Power and battery) and choose the best performance mode while plugged in.

## 3. Make sure the right graphics chip is used

Laptops with two graphics chips can run Minecraft on the weaker one by mistake. Open Windows Settings, System, Display, Graphics, add the Java program your launcher uses (often `javaw.exe`), choose Options and set it to **High performance**. Then restart the game.

## 4. Use Java 21 and sensible memory

Minecraft 1.21.1 needs Java 21, see the [Java 21 guide](/blog/install-java-21-for-minecraft-1-21-1/). Many laptops have 8 GB of RAM, so around 3 to 4 GB for the game is usually enough. Use the [RAM calculator](/tools/minecraft-ram-calculator/).

## 5. Lower the heavy settings

Reduce render distance and simulation distance, use Fast graphics and minimal particles. The [video settings generator](/tools/minecraft-settings-generator/) gives starting values for a low-end or mid-range PC.

## 6. Add performance mods

Fabric optimisation mods from Modrinth can raise frame rates a lot on laptops. Follow the [mods guide](/blog/install-fabric-mods-modrinth-minecraft-1-21-1/) and the [FPS guide](/blog/boost-fps-minecraft-1-21-1-fabric/).

## 7. Keep it cool

A hot laptop slows itself down. Use it on a hard surface, clean the vents and avoid blocking airflow.

## 8. Close other programs

Browsers with many tabs, recorders and overlays compete for memory and the graphics chip.

## Measure the change

Turn on an FPS counter in the [FireClient HUD](/blog/fireclient-hud-setup-guide/), write down the number before you change anything and check it after each step.

posts.title: Fabric vs Forge vs NeoForge vs Quilt: which mod loader for 1.21.1?
posts.metaTitle: Fabric vs Forge vs NeoForge vs Quilt for Minecraft 1.21.1
posts.metaDescription: Compare Fabric, Forge, NeoForge and Quilt for Minecraft 1.21.1: performance, mod choice, updates and how to pick the right mod loader for your PC.
posts.excerpt: What each Minecraft mod loader is for, how they differ, and a simple way to choose for 1.21.1.
posts.body:
A **mod loader** is the software that lets Minecraft load mods. Fabric, Forge, NeoForge and Quilt all do that job, but a mod built for one will not run on another. Here is how to choose for Minecraft 1.21.1.

## The short version

- **Fabric** is lightweight and quick to support new Minecraft versions. It has a large scene of performance and quality-of-life mods.
- **Forge** is the long-established loader with a very large library of older and large-scale mods.
- **NeoForge** began as a fork of Forge and is the Forge-style option that is actively developed for newer versions.
- **Quilt** is a fork of Fabric that can run many Fabric mods, with a smaller community.

## How to choose

1. **Start from the mods you want.** Open the mod's page on [Modrinth](https://modrinth.com) and see which loaders and versions it lists for **1.21.1**. The loader is decided by the mod, not the other way round.
2. **Do not mix loaders.** A Fabric mod will not load on Forge or NeoForge, and the reverse is also true.
3. **Pick Fabric for performance and light setups.** Fabric is the usual base for frame-rate and utility mods. See the [FPS guide](/blog/boost-fps-minecraft-1-21-1-fabric/).
4. **Pick Forge or NeoForge for big content mods.** If the mods you want are large content packs that only support those loaders, use the loader they require.

## What about performance?

The loader matters less than the mods you run and your settings. A light Fabric setup with a few optimisation mods often feels smooth on modest PCs, but a heavy list of mods will be demanding on any loader. Use the [RAM calculator](/tools/minecraft-ram-calculator/) to pick a memory setting.

## Which one does FireClient use?

The FireClient in-game client is built for **Minecraft 1.21.1 on Fabric with Java 21**. You can still launch other versions without the FireClient mod. The [mods guide](/blog/install-fabric-mods-modrinth-minecraft-1-21-1/) shows how to pick the right files, and the [explainer](/blog/what-is-a-minecraft-client-fabric-explained/) covers launchers, loaders and clients.

## Quick rules

- One loader per profile
- Install the loader's API mod if the mods ask for it, such as Fabric API
- Keep separate profiles for separate loaders
- [Back up your worlds](/blog/backup-minecraft-worlds-windows/) before changing loaders

posts.author: FirePDX
posts.title: How to fix "Connection timed out" and "Failed to connect" in Minecraft
posts.metaTitle: Fix Minecraft Connection Timed Out and Failed to Connect
posts.metaDescription: Minecraft says connection timed out or failed to connect? Check the address, version, firewall, VPN, DNS and router, whether you play or host the server.
posts.excerpt: A checklist for "Connection timed out", "Connection refused" and "Failed to connect to the server" in Minecraft 1.21.1.
posts.body:
"Connection timed out" and "Failed to connect to the server" usually mean your game cannot reach the server, or the server cannot accept you. Start with the checks for players, then see the section for people who host.

## If you are joining a server

1. **Check the address and port.** A typo is the most common cause. If the server uses a port other than 25565, add it after a colon.
2. **Check the version.** Your game must match the server. For 1.21.1, use a 1.21.1 profile, and check the server's required version.
3. **Check that the server is online.** Ask the owner, or check the server's website or Discord.
4. **Restart your router and PC.** This clears many network glitches.
5. **Turn off VPN or proxy.** Try again without them.
6. **Check Windows Firewall and security software.** Make sure Java is allowed.
7. **Try another network.** A phone hotspot shows whether your home network or school network is the problem.
8. **Check mods.** A mod that changes networking can break joining. Test with a clean profile, as in the [crash checklist](/blog/fix-minecraft-crash-fabric-1-21-1/).
9. **Check whitelist and bans.** Some servers only accept listed players.

## If you host the server

- Join `localhost` first. If that fails, the server is not running correctly.
- Forward TCP **25565** to the PC, allow Java in the firewall, and check you are using your public IP address.
- If your provider uses CGNAT, port forwarding cannot work.

The full steps are in the [Paper server guide](/blog/host-minecraft-paper-server-windows/).

## Read the error text

"Connection refused" means something answered but did not accept, which often points to a wrong port or a server that is not running. "Timed out" means nothing answered, which often points to a firewall, router or wrong address.

## Get help

Ask in the [FireClient Discord](https://discord.gg/r23YNWWfrx) and share only the error text. Never post tokens, account files or your router login.

posts.author: FirePDX
posts.title: How to host a Minecraft Paper server on Windows
posts.metaTitle: Host a Minecraft Paper Server on Windows (1.21.1)
posts.metaDescription: Host a Paper server for Minecraft 1.21.1 on Windows: Java 21, EULA, port forwarding on 25565, firewall, whitelist and safety tips for playing with friends.
posts.excerpt: Run a Paper server on your PC for friends: Java 21, the EULA, port forwarding, the firewall and basic safety.
posts.body:
A Paper server lets you and your friends play together on a world you control. This guide covers hosting one on a Windows PC for Minecraft 1.21.1. [FireClient](/download/) can run a Paper server from the launcher and shows Running once Paper reports ready, but router port forwarding is still up to you.

## 1. Check the basics

You need Java 21 (see the [Java 21 guide](/blog/install-java-21-for-minecraft-1-21-1/)), enough free memory for the server plus the game, and a PC that stays on while friends play.

## 2. Start the server once

Start the Paper server from your launcher or by running the Paper jar. The first run creates the server files. Minecraft's EULA must be accepted before a server will run. If your launcher does not ask, read the EULA, then open `eula.txt` in the server folder and set `eula=true`.

## 3. Join it yourself

Start Minecraft 1.21.1 and join `localhost`. If that works, the server itself is fine.

## 4. Let friends connect from the internet

Friends outside your home network need your router to send traffic to your PC.

- Give your PC a fixed local address in your router settings
- Forward TCP port **25565** to that address
- Allow Java through Windows Firewall when Windows asks
- Share your public IP address only with people you trust

If your internet provider shares one public address between many customers (CGNAT), port forwarding will not work. Ask your provider or use a hosting service instead.

## 5. Keep it private and safe

- Keep `online-mode=true` in `server.properties`, so only real accounts can join
- Turn on the whitelist with `white-list=true`, then add friends with `/whitelist add name`
- Keep Paper updated and install only plugins you trust
- Do not expose admin or remote-control ports to the internet

## 6. Protect the world

[Back up your world](/blog/backup-minecraft-worlds-windows/) before changing plugins or versions. Lower the view distance in `server.properties` if the PC struggles, and see the [FPS guide](/blog/boost-fps-minecraft-1-21-1-fabric/) for game-side tips.

## If friends cannot connect

Use the [connection timed out checklist](/blog/fix-minecraft-connection-timed-out/). Ask for help in the [FireClient Discord](https://discord.gg/r23YNWWfrx) and never post your router login or account tokens.

posts.author: FirePDX
posts.title: How to fix Minecraft Microsoft sign-in errors on Windows
posts.metaTitle: Fix Minecraft Microsoft Sign-In Errors on Windows
posts.metaDescription: Can't sign in to Minecraft with your Microsoft account? Check date and time, Java Edition ownership, family settings and network, then retry safely.
posts.excerpt: Practical checks for Minecraft Microsoft sign-in errors, from your PC clock to family settings, plus how to stay safe.
posts.body:
If a launcher cannot sign you in with Microsoft, the cause is usually the PC clock, the account itself or the network. Work through these checks in order.

## 1. Check your internet and service status

Make sure other sites load. If they do, check the Xbox service status page, because Minecraft sign-in uses Microsoft, Xbox and Minecraft services and an outage there is not something you can fix.

## 2. Fix your date and time

Open Windows Settings, Time and language, Date and time, and turn on automatic time and time zone. A wrong clock can make secure sign-in fail.

## 3. Confirm the account owns Minecraft Java Edition

To play online you need your own Minecraft Java Edition account. Sign in at minecraft.net with the same Microsoft account and check that Java Edition is on it. A different account from the one you bought with is a common cause. See the [Java vs Bedrock guide](/blog/minecraft-java-vs-bedrock-which-edition/) if you are not sure which edition you own.

## 4. Check family settings for child accounts

Child accounts need an adult in the Microsoft family group to allow online play and multiplayer. Ask the family organiser to review the account's Xbox privacy and family settings.

## 5. Sign out and sign back in

Remove the account in your launcher, close it and add it again. Then restart the launcher and try once more.

## 6. Turn off VPN or proxy

Try without a VPN or proxy, because they can block or change sign-in requests.

## 7. Test your Microsoft account in a browser

Sign in at account.microsoft.com. If the password, two-step check or a security prompt fails there, fix that first.

## 8. Update the launcher

Install the latest version from the [official download page](/download/). The [launcher fix guide](/blog/minecraft-launcher-not-opening-windows/) covers problems that stop it from starting.

## Stay safe

- Enter your password only on a genuine Microsoft sign-in page
- Never share access tokens, account files or your launcher data folder
- Be wary of anyone offering to "fix" sign-in by asking for your login
- FireClient says it keeps account token data locally in protected form, and the [Terms and Privacy notice](/terms-and-privacy.html) explains what is sent to Microsoft

If it still fails, ask in the [FireClient Discord](https://discord.gg/r23YNWWfrx) and describe the error without posting tokens or logs with personal paths.

posts.author: FirePDX
posts.title: How to find safe Minecraft mods (and avoid fake ones)
posts.metaTitle: How to Find Safe Minecraft Mods and Avoid Fake Downloads
posts.metaDescription: Download Minecraft mods safely: use trusted platforms like Modrinth, check the loader and version, read the page, and avoid .exe files and random links.
posts.excerpt: A short safety checklist for Minecraft mod downloads: trusted sources, version checks and red flags to avoid.
posts.body:
Most Minecraft mods are made by hobbyists in good faith, but fake download pages and bad files do exist. This checklist helps you pick mods that are safer and more likely to work.

## 1. Use a trusted platform

Download from a well-known mod platform such as [Modrinth](https://modrinth.com) rather than a random link from a video description, a chat message or a file-sharing site. The mod manager in [FireClient](/download/) can browse Modrinth directly.

## 2. Remember what a mod file looks like

A Fabric mod is a **.jar** file that goes in your mods folder. A mod is not an installer. If something calls itself a mod but you have to run an **.exe**, a **.bat** or a **.msi**, do not run it.

## 3. Check version and loader

Open the Versions tab and filter for **Minecraft 1.21.1** and **Fabric**. The [mods guide](/blog/install-fabric-mods-modrinth-minecraft-1-21-1/) shows how. A wrong version is the most common reason for a crash.

## 4. Read the project page

Look for a clear description, a source code link, an issue tracker, recent updates and a reasonable number of downloads. A page with no description, copied text or only a download button is a warning sign.

## 5. Check the dependencies

Many mods need Fabric API or another mod. Install only the required ones the page lists.

## 6. Be careful with unknown authors

For a new or unknown author, read comments and issues and start with well-known mods first.

## 7. Test and keep a backup

Add one mod at a time and [back up your worlds](/blog/backup-minecraft-worlds-windows/) before big changes. If the game crashes, use the [crash checklist](/blog/fix-minecraft-crash-fabric-1-21-1/).

## If something looks wrong

If you ran a file you now doubt, run a scan with Windows Security, change your Microsoft account password and review your account activity. Never share access tokens or account files with anyone.

posts.title: Best Minecraft settings for PvP on 1.21.1 (Java Edition)
posts.metaTitle: Best Minecraft PvP Settings for 1.21.1 (FPS, Mouse, HUD)
posts.metaDescription: Set up Minecraft 1.21.1 for PvP: stable FPS, raw mouse input, sensible distances, a clean HUD with FPS and coordinates, and respect for server rules.
posts.excerpt: Video, mouse and HUD settings that give steadier frames and cleaner information in Minecraft 1.21.1 PvP.
posts.body:
Good PvP comes down to steady frames, predictable mouse input and a screen that shows what you need. These settings are a starting point for Minecraft Java Edition 1.21.1. Adjust them to your PC and your taste.

## 1. Aim for steady frames

A high, stable frame rate helps more than a high peak. Lower render distance to around 8 to 12 chunks, turn off fancy graphics and reduce particles. The [FPS guide](/blog/boost-fps-minecraft-1-21-1-fabric/) covers memory, Java 21 and Fabric performance mods.

## 2. Use raw mouse input

In Options, Controls, Mouse Settings, turn on **Raw Input** so the game reads your mouse directly. Then set sensitivity to something you can repeat, and keep it the same across sessions.

## 3. Pick a comfortable field of view

A wider FOV shows more of the fight, and a narrower one makes targets larger. Test a few values and keep the one you aim best with.

## 4. Limit visual noise

Turn off clouds, lower biome blend and keep particles minimal, so fast action is easy to read.

## 5. Build a clean HUD

Show only what you use. FPS and coordinates are common choices, and too many elements crowd the screen. In [FireClient](/blog/fireclient-hud-setup-guide/) you can drag each HUD element where you want it and keep the rest off. [Back up your layout](/blog/back-up-fireclient-hud-layout/) once you are happy.

## 6. Check your connection and PC

Close background apps, use a wired connection if you can and check your ping on the server you play on.

## 7. Follow the server's rules

Some servers restrict certain client features or mods. Read the rules before you join and use only what is allowed. No setting replaces practice, and these changes just remove avoidable obstacles.

posts.author: FirePDX
posts.title: Minecraft launcher not opening on Windows? Try these fixes
posts.metaTitle: Launcher Not Opening on Windows: Safe Fixes
posts.metaDescription: A Minecraft launcher that will not open on Windows 10 or 11 is usually blocked, stuck or damaged. Work through these safe fixes, including SmartScreen and reinstalling.
posts.excerpt: Safe steps for a launcher that does nothing when you click it, from stuck processes to SmartScreen and reinstalling.
posts.body:
If a launcher does nothing when you open it, the cause is usually a stuck process, a blocked file or a damaged install. These steps are safe to try in order, and they apply to most Windows launchers, including [FireClient](/download/).

## 1. Restart and try again

Close the launcher, restart your PC and open it once. A leftover background process from an earlier crash is a common cause.

## 2. End a stuck process

Press Ctrl + Shift + Esc to open Task Manager. If you see the launcher listed, right-click it and choose End task, then open it again.

## 3. Check that the file is not blocked

Right-click the installer or the launcher file, choose Properties and look for an Unblock checkbox near the bottom of the General tab. Tick it and press OK. Only do this for a file you downloaded from an official source, and verify it first with the steps in the [safety guide](/blog/is-fireclient-safe/).

## 4. Look at SmartScreen and antivirus

Windows SmartScreen or your antivirus can stop an unsigned installer from running. The FireClient early access installer is unsigned, so a prompt is expected. If you have verified the SHA-256 and downloaded from the official page, you can choose to run it. If you are not sure, do not run it.

## 5. Check your system

FireClient needs Windows 10 or 11 (64-bit). Make sure Windows is up to date and you have free disk space.

## 6. Reinstall cleanly

Uninstall the launcher in Windows Settings, restart, download a fresh copy from the [official download page](/download/) and install again. Your worlds are not stored in the installer folder, but [back up your worlds](/blog/backup-minecraft-worlds-windows/) first to be safe.

## 7. Ask for help

If it still fails, ask in the [FireClient Discord](https://discord.gg/r23YNWWfrx). Say your Windows version and what happens when you click. Never post account files or access tokens.

posts.author: FirePDX
posts.title: What is a Minecraft client? Launcher, Fabric and mods explained
posts.metaTitle: What Is a Minecraft Client? Fabric and Mods Explained
posts.metaDescription: Minecraft launcher, client, mod loader and mod: what each term means, how Fabric fits in, and how FireClient combines a launcher with a Fabric client.
posts.excerpt: Four terms people mix up, explained simply: launcher, client, mod loader and mod.
posts.body:
People use "launcher", "client" and "mod" as if they mean the same thing. They do not. Here is what each one is, and how they fit together.

## Launcher

A **launcher** is the program that signs you in, picks a game version and starts Minecraft. It also manages profiles, memory settings and game files. The standard Minecraft Launcher is one example, and [FireClient](/download/) includes a launcher too.

## Mod loader

A **mod loader** is software that lets Minecraft load mods. **Fabric** is a lightweight mod loader that is popular for fast updates to new Minecraft versions. Other loaders include Forge, NeoForge and Quilt. A mod must be built for the loader you use.

## Mod

A **mod** is a file that changes or adds something to the game, such as better performance or a new interface. Mods are usually shared on sites like [Modrinth](https://modrinth.com). See the [mods guide](/blog/install-fabric-mods-modrinth-minecraft-1-21-1/) for how to pick the right file.

## Client

A **client** is a package of features that runs inside the game, often for quality-of-life and display tweaks. Examples include a customisable HUD with FPS, coordinates and other readouts, or a menu to switch settings. A client is built on top of a mod loader.

## How FireClient fits

FireClient combines a launcher with a Fabric client. The launcher starts Minecraft Java Edition on Windows, and the in-game client adds a draggable HUD and a menu that opens with Right Shift, for Minecraft 1.21.1 on Fabric with Java 21. Set up the HUD in the [HUD guide](/blog/fireclient-hud-setup-guide/).

## One more thing

Some servers have rules about which client features are allowed. Read a server's rules before you join, and respect them.

posts.author: FirePDX
posts.title: How to back up your Minecraft worlds on Windows
posts.metaTitle: How to Back Up Minecraft Worlds on Windows (Java Edition)
posts.metaDescription: Back up Minecraft Java worlds before updates or mods: find the saves folder, copy the world while the game is closed, zip it with a date and restore it later.
posts.excerpt: Copy, date and store your Minecraft worlds safely before you change mods or update the game.
posts.body:
A world can be lost to a bad mod, a crash or a mistake. A two-minute backup protects hours of building. This guide covers Minecraft Java Edition on Windows.

## 1. Close the game

Quit Minecraft completely so no files are being written. Copying a world while the game is open can produce a damaged backup.

## 2. Find your saves folder

In the standard Minecraft setup, worlds are in `%appdata%\.minecraft\saves`. Paste that into the File Explorer address bar and press Enter. Each folder inside is one world. A launcher that uses a different game folder will show its own saves folder, so check your launcher's settings. The worlds library in [FireClient](/early-access/) lists your worlds with an icon, save date and size, which helps you pick the right one.

## 3. Copy the world

Right-click the world folder, choose copy, and paste it somewhere else, such as Documents. For a smaller file, right-click the copy and choose Send to, Compressed (zipped) folder.

## 4. Name it with the date

Rename the backup with the world name and date, for example `Survival-2026-10-17`. Keep a few older copies, not only the latest one.

## 5. Keep one copy off your PC

Put a copy on an external drive or in cloud storage, so a dead drive does not take both copies.

## When to back up

- Before installing or removing mods
- Before updating Minecraft or changing the Fabric version
- Before testing a large build or redstone project

## How to restore

Close the game, delete or rename the broken world folder in `saves`, then paste your backup folder in its place. Open the game and the world appears in the list.

For settings rather than worlds, see how to [back up your FireClient HUD layout](/blog/back-up-fireclient-hud-layout/).

posts.metaTitle: Install Java 21 for Minecraft 1.21.1 on Windows
posts.metaDescription: Minecraft 1.21.1 needs Java 21. Check your Java version, install a trusted Java 21 build on Windows 10 or 11, and fix common Java errors.
posts.excerpt: Check your Java version, install Java 21 on Windows, and fix the most common Java errors for Minecraft 1.21.1.
posts.body:
Minecraft 1.21.1 runs on **Java 21**. Older Java versions can stop the game from starting. This guide shows how to check what you have and install the right one on Windows 10 or 11.

## 1. Check your current Java version

Press the Windows key, type `cmd` and open Command Prompt. Type `java -version` and press Enter. If the first line shows a version that starts with 21, you are ready. If it shows 8, 11 or 17, or says Java is not recognised, continue.

## 2. Download Java 21

Download a **Java 21** build for **Windows x64** from a trusted vendor. Eclipse Temurin and the Microsoft Build of OpenJDK are common choices. Pick the **JDK or JRE 21** installer (.msi) and avoid unknown download sites.

## 3. Install it

Run the installer. If it offers options such as adding Java to PATH or setting JAVA_HOME, enable them. Finish the install.

## 4. Check again

Close Command Prompt, open a new one and run `java -version`. It should now show version 21.

## 5. Restart your launcher

Close and reopen your launcher so it picks up the new Java. In [FireClient](/download/), start the Minecraft 1.21.1 Fabric profile and check that it opens.

## Common problems

- **Still shows an old version.** Another Java install is earlier in your PATH. Uninstall the old one in Windows Settings, then check again.
- **"Java not found".** Reinstall and make sure the PATH option was enabled.
- **Game still crashes.** Follow the [crash checklist](/blog/fix-minecraft-crash-fabric-1-21-1/).

Always download installers from the vendor's official site and never from a video description or file-sharing link. The [safety guide](/blog/is-fireclient-safe/) explains how to verify a file with SHA-256.

posts.title: How to fix Minecraft crashing on launch (Fabric 1.21.1)
posts.metaTitle: Fix Minecraft Crashing on Launch: Fabric 1.21.1 Checklist
posts.metaDescription: Minecraft 1.21.1 crashes on launch with Fabric? Work through this checklist: Java 21, mod versions, Fabric API, memory, drivers and how to read the crash report.
posts.excerpt: A step-by-step checklist for Minecraft 1.21.1 crashes on Fabric, from Java version to reading the crash report.
posts.body:
If Minecraft 1.21.1 closes right after you press Play, work through this list in order. Most Fabric crashes come from a mismatched mod, the wrong Java version or a missing dependency.

## 1. Check your Java version

Minecraft 1.21.1 needs **Java 21**. Open Command Prompt and type `java -version`. If it shows an older version, follow the [Java 21 guide](/blog/install-java-21-for-minecraft-1-21-1/).

## 2. Remove the last mod you added

Move the newest mod out of your mods folder and launch again. If the game starts, that mod was the cause. Look for a newer file that supports 1.21.1.

## 3. Check every mod's version and loader

Each mod must list **Minecraft 1.21.1** and **Fabric**. Files for Forge, NeoForge, Quilt or a different Minecraft version will not load. The [Modrinth mods guide](/blog/install-fabric-mods-modrinth-minecraft-1-21-1/) shows how to filter for the right file.

## 4. Make sure Fabric API is installed

Many mods need Fabric API. If a crash report says a dependency is missing, install the version that matches 1.21.1.

## 5. Test with no mods

Launch a clean 1.21.1 Fabric profile with only Fabric API. If that works, add mods back one at a time.

## 6. Review your memory setting

Too little memory can crash heavy mod setups, and a huge value can also cause trouble on low-RAM PCs. Around 4 GB is a safe starting point for most Fabric setups. See the [RAM guide](/blog/minecraft-ram-allocation-guide/).

## 7. Update your graphics driver

Crashes on startup that mention graphics or OpenGL are often fixed by updating your GPU driver from the manufacturer.

## 8. Read the crash report

Minecraft writes a crash report when it fails. In the standard setup it is saved in the `crash-reports` folder inside your game folder. Look near the top for the mod name and for lines starting with "Caused by".

## Ask for help the safe way

Share only the relevant part of the report in the [FireClient Discord](https://discord.gg/r23YNWWfrx). Never post account files, access tokens or unredacted logs that contain personal paths.

posts.title: Minecraft Java vs Bedrock: which edition should you play?
posts.metaTitle: Minecraft Java vs Bedrock: Differences and Which to Pick
posts.metaDescription: Java or Bedrock? Compare platforms, mods, servers and cross-play, learn how to check which edition you own, and see which one FireClient supports.
posts.excerpt: Platforms, mods, servers and cross-play compared in plain language, plus how to tell which edition you own.
posts.body:
Minecraft comes in two main versions for most players: **Java Edition** and **Bedrock Edition**. They share the same core game but differ in platforms, mods, servers and how you launch them. Here is a plain comparison so you can pick the one that fits.

## Quick comparison

- **Platforms.** Java runs on Windows, macOS and Linux. Bedrock runs on Windows, consoles, phones and tablets.
- **Mods.** Java has a large mod scene through loaders such as Fabric and Forge. Bedrock uses add-ons and Marketplace content instead of mods.
- **Servers.** Java has a huge community-server scene, including servers built on Paper. Bedrock has its own server ecosystem and featured servers.
- **Cross-play.** Bedrock players can usually play with friends across consoles, phones and PC. Java players play with other Java players.
- **Launcher.** Java starts from a launcher, which is where tools such as [FireClient](/download/) come in. Bedrock on Windows starts from its own app.

## How to tell which one you own

Java Edition starts from the Minecraft Launcher and shows a Java Edition title. Bedrock Edition on Windows starts from the Microsoft Store app. If you bought the PC version, check your Microsoft account, because the PC purchase often includes both editions.

## Which should you pick?

Pick **Java** if you want mods, custom launchers, the classic server scene or a customisable HUD. Pick **Bedrock** if you play on a console or phone, or want cross-play with friends on other devices. You can own both and switch.

## Where FireClient fits

FireClient is for **Java Edition on Windows 10 and 11**. It does not run on Bedrock, MCPE, phones, consoles, macOS or Linux, as explained in the [Bedrock and MCPE guide](/blog/fireclient-minecraft-bedrock-mcpe/). If you play Java on a Windows PC, start with the [install guide](/blog/install-fireclient-windows/).

Look for an official site, a public release page and a published checksum. Be careful with launchers shared through video descriptions or reupload sites. Our own [safety guide](/blog/is-fireclient-safe/) shows how to verify an installer.

## 2. Real account handling

A launcher should let you sign in with your own Microsoft account for online play, and should be clear about what it stores. Avoid anything that asks you to paste access tokens.

## 3. Mod and version management

Check whether it supports the loader you use (Fabric, Forge and others), whether it can browse Modrinth, and whether it keeps separate profiles so one broken mod does not ruin everything.

## 4. Memory and performance controls

You should be able to set the memory budget without editing command lines. See the [RAM guide](/blog/minecraft-ram-allocation-guide/) for sensible numbers.

## 5. Worlds, resource packs and backups

A good launcher shows your worlds and helps you keep them safe when you update or uninstall.

## 6. Honest limits

Read what the project says it cannot do yet. Marketing that promises everything is a warning sign.

## Where FireClient fits

FireClient is a free launcher for Minecraft Java Edition on Windows 10 and 11, with a Fabric in-game client for 1.21.1. It has a draggable HUD with 11 elements, 3 accent themes, a Modrinth mod manager, a worlds library, a memory setting, local skins and Paper server hosting.

Mods for Minecraft 1.21.1 only work if they match your game version and mod loader. This guide covers the checks that prevent most crashes, and how the FireClient mod manager fits in.

- The Fabric loader for 1.21.1

## Pick the right file on Modrinth

On a mod page at [Modrinth](https://modrinth.com), open the Versions tab and filter by **1.21.1** and **Fabric**. A file for another Minecraft version or another loader (Forge, NeoForge, Quilt) will not load on your setup. Read the dependencies list on the page and install anything marked required.

The FireClient launcher has a mods page with Modrinth browsing, your own jar files, and curated packs for Performance, Visuals, Utility and PvP. Use it to add mods to your Minecraft 1.21.1 Fabric profile so the files land in the right folder. Make sure the profile is set to 1.21.1 Fabric before you add anything. See the [install guide](/blog/install-fireclient-windows/) if you have not set up the launcher yet.

Add one mod, launch the game, and check that it opens. Then add the next. When something crashes, you know which mod caused it. Installing twenty at once and guessing is the slow way.

- Remove the last mod you added and start again
- Check that every mod lists 1.21.1 and Fabric, and that Fabric API is present
- Read the crash report for the mod name near the top, and look for a missing dependency

posts.title: How to boost FPS in Minecraft 1.21.1 on Fabric
posts.metaTitle: Boost FPS in Minecraft 1.21.1 on Fabric: Practical Steps
posts.metaDescription: Raise Minecraft 1.21.1 FPS on Fabric: lower render distance, set sensible RAM, use well-known Fabric performance mods from Modrinth, and measure with an FPS HUD.
posts.excerpt: Settings, memory and performance mods that raise FPS in Minecraft 1.21.1, plus how to measure the change with the FireClient HUD.
posts.body:
Low FPS in Minecraft 1.21.1 usually comes from a few causes you can fix: view distance, memory, background apps and missing optimisation mods. Work through the list below, changing one thing at a time so you can see what helped.

## 1. Measure first

Turn on the FPS element on your [FireClient HUD](/blog/fireclient-hud-setup-guide/) and play the same world for a few minutes before you change anything. Write the number down. Without a baseline you cannot tell what worked.

## 2. Lower the distance settings

Render distance and simulation distance have the biggest effect on most PCs. Try 10 to 12 chunks for render distance, and 6 to 8 for simulation distance, then raise them if you have headroom. Fancy graphics, smooth lighting and high particle settings cost frames too.

## 3. Set sensible memory

More RAM is not always faster. For Fabric with performance mods, around 4 GB is a comfortable start. Our [RAM guide](/blog/minecraft-ram-allocation-guide/) explains how to pick a number and where to set it in the launcher.

## 4. Use Java 21

Minecraft 1.21.1 runs on Java 21. An old Java runtime can cause slower performance or refuse to start the game at all.

## 5. Add performance mods from Modrinth

Fabric has well-known optimisation mods on [Modrinth](https://modrinth.com), including Sodium for rendering, Lithium for game logic and FerriteCore for memory use. Always open the mod page and check that it lists Minecraft 1.21.1 and Fabric before you install it. The FireClient launcher has a mod manager with Modrinth support and a curated Performance pack. The [mods guide](/blog/install-fabric-mods-modrinth-minecraft-1-21-1/) shows the steps.

## 6. Close what you do not need

Browsers with many tabs, screen recorders and overlays compete for memory and GPU time. Close them while you test, and make sure your laptop is plugged in and not on a battery saver plan.

## 7. Compare and keep what works

Check your FPS number again after each change. If something made no difference or caused crashes, undo it. Results depend heavily on your CPU, GPU and the mods you run, so treat the numbers here as a starting point, not a promise.

posts.title: Is FireClient safe? How to check your download
posts.metaTitle: Is FireClient Safe? How to Verify the Installer
posts.metaDescription: Is FireClient safe to install? Where the official download lives, why the beta installer is unsigned, and how to check its SHA-256 before you run it.
posts.excerpt: The official download sources, why Windows may warn you, and a 30-second hash check you can do before running the installer.
posts.body:
People search "is FireClient safe" for a good reason: any Minecraft client installer deserves a second look before you run it. This page tells you exactly where the official download lives, what is unusual about the current build, and how to check your file yourself. It is not a guarantee, and you should make the call with the facts.

## Official sources only

Download FireClient from [fireclient.net](/download/) or from the official [GitHub Releases page](https://github.com/untitledinfo/verifed-fireclient/releases). If a file comes from a video description, a random mirror or a Discord direct message, do not run it. Links on this site point to the GitHub release file.

## Why Windows may show a warning

The current early access installer is unsigned. We do not have a paid code-signing certificate yet, so Windows SmartScreen can show a prompt for an app it does not recognise. That prompt is expected for a new unsigned installer. It does not prove the file is safe, and it does not prove it is unsafe. It means Windows has no reputation data for it yet.

## Check the SHA-256 yourself

A hash is a fingerprint of a file. If your copy has the same SHA-256 as the one published on the [download page](/download/), the file was not changed on the way to you. In PowerShell:

```
Get-FileHash .\FireClient-Setup.exe -Algorithm SHA256
```

Compare the result with the hash shown on the download page. If they differ, delete the file and download it again from an official source.

## Good habits for any Minecraft client

- Never paste your Microsoft or Minecraft access token, account files or unredacted logs into a public chat
- Read what the app asks permission for, and read the [Terms and Privacy notice](/terms-and-privacy.html)
- Keep a backup of worlds you care about before changing game files
- Scan the file with Windows Security or your own antivirus if you want another opinion

## What FireClient needs from you

To play online you need your own Minecraft Java Edition account. FireClient does not give you the game for free. See the [install guide](/blog/install-fireclient-windows/) for the full steps, and ask in the [Discord](https://discord.gg/r23YNWWfrx) if something looks wrong.

posts.title: How to set up the FireClient HUD in Minecraft 1.21.1
posts.excerpt: Open the FireClient menu with Right Shift, switch on the HUD elements you want and drag them into place with the HUD editor.
posts.body:
FireClient adds a HUD and an in-game menu to Minecraft 1.21.1 on Fabric. This guide covers how to open the menu, turn elements on, move them, and where your layout is saved.

## Open the menu

Start a Minecraft 1.21.1 Fabric world and press **Right Shift**. You can also use the **FireClient Menu** button on the title screen. The menu has four tabs: HUD, Features, Theme and About.

## Choose your HUD elements

The HUD tab has a switch for each element. FireClient includes eleven:

- Watermark
- FPS
- Coordinates
- Ping
- Direction
- Memory
- Clock
- Keystrokes
- Armor
- Effects
- CPS

Turn on only what you read during play. A short list keeps the screen clear, whether you are in a PvP match or building.

![FireClient HUD settings with a toggle for each element](/assets/ingame-hud-960.jpg)

## Move things with the HUD editor

Press **Edit HUD Positions** and drag each element where you want it. Positions, visibility and the sprint toggle are saved to `config/fireclient/client.json`, so your layout is the same the next time you launch.

## Pick an accent theme

The Theme tab has three accent themes. You can switch at any time, and the change shows up in the menu and HUD right away.

## Keep the layout tidy

Start with three or four elements and add more only if you miss them. Leave the middle of the screen clear so the HUD never covers what you are aiming at. If elements end up off screen after you change resolution, open the menu with **Right Shift** and use **Edit HUD Positions** to drag them back.

## If the menu does not open

The FireClient menu only exists in the in-game client, which is built for Minecraft 1.21.1 on Fabric with Java 21. Check that you launched that version, because the launcher can start other versions but they run without the FireClient mod. You can also use the **FireClient Menu** button on the title screen. If the game crashes on start, see the [Fabric crash checklist](/blog/fix-minecraft-crash-fabric-1-21-1/), and if Java is the problem, [install Java 21](/blog/install-java-21-for-minecraft-1-21-1/).

## What you need

The in-game client is built for Minecraft 1.21.1 on Fabric with Java 21. The launcher can start other versions, but they launch without the FireClient mod.

## Next steps

- [Back up and reuse your HUD layout](/blog/back-up-fireclient-hud-layout/) so you never set it up twice
- [Best settings for PvP on 1.21.1](/blog/best-minecraft-pvp-settings-1-21-1/)
- [Boost FPS on 1.21.1 with Fabric](/blog/boost-fps-minecraft-1-21-1-fabric/)
- [Install FireClient on Windows in five steps](/blog/install-fireclient-windows/)

Questions? Ask in the [FireClient Discord](https://discord.gg/r23YNWWfrx), or [download FireClient](/#download) to try the HUD yourself.

posts.metaDescription: How much RAM to give Minecraft: sensible starting points for vanilla, Fabric performance mods and big modpacks, plus how to set memory in FireClient.
posts.body:
Giving Minecraft more memory does not always make it faster. Too little causes stutters and crashes. Too much can make garbage collection pauses longer and starves the rest of your PC. This guide gives sensible starting points and shows where the setting lives in FireClient.

## Quick starting points

These are rules of thumb, not guarantees. Mods, shaders and view distance change the picture.

- Vanilla Minecraft 1.21: 2 to 4 GB is usually enough
- Performance mods on Fabric: 4 GB is a comfortable start
- Large modpacks or heavy shaders: 6 to 8 GB, raised only if you actually run out

## Do not give it everything

Leave at least 2 to 4 GB for Windows and your other apps. If your PC has 8 GB in total, 4 GB for Minecraft is a sensible ceiling. Asking for more than your system can spare pushes memory onto the disk, which is slower than a smaller allocation.

## Set it in FireClient

In the launcher settings, choose a memory budget. FireClient passes it to Java as the maximum heap and limits it to a safe range, so an extreme value cannot be set by mistake.

## Signs you need more, or less

- Crashes with an out-of-memory error, or stutters that get worse over time: raise it by 1 GB and test again
- Short freezes every few seconds on a high setting: try lowering it
- Slow loading while other apps compete for memory: close them or reduce the amount

## Check your result

Change one thing at a time. Keep the FPS and Memory elements on your [FireClient HUD](/blog/fireclient-hud-setup-guide/) while you play for ten minutes, then compare. If you are new to the launcher, start with the [install guide](/blog/install-fireclient-windows/).

posts.title: Back up and reuse your FireClient HUD layout
posts.metaTitle: Back Up Your FireClient HUD Layout (client.json)
posts.excerpt: Your HUD layout lives in one small file. Copy it to keep a backup or to move your setup to another PC.
posts.metaDescription: Back up your FireClient HUD layout by copying client.json, and move your HUD setup to another PC. Includes how to fix elements that end up off screen.
posts.body:
Your HUD layout takes a few minutes to set up, so it is worth backing up. FireClient keeps it in one small file.

## Where the layout is stored

Positions, visibility and the sprint toggle are saved to `config/fireclient/client.json`. The path is relative to your Minecraft game folder, so look for a `config` folder inside it, then `fireclient`.

## Back it up

1. Close Minecraft so the file is not being written.
2. Copy `client.json` to a safe place, such as a cloud folder or a USB drive.
3. Put a date in the copy's name, for example `client-2026-10-13.json`, so you can keep a few versions.

## Reuse it on another PC

Install FireClient on the other PC and run Minecraft 1.21.1 on Fabric once, so the `config/fireclient` folder exists. Close the game, then put your copy in that folder as `client.json`. The layout should load the next time you start the game. Keep a copy of the original first in case you want to go back.

## When something looks wrong

If elements end up off screen after a resolution change, open the menu with **Right Shift** and use **Edit HUD Positions** to drag them back. The [HUD setup guide](/blog/fireclient-hud-setup-guide/) has the full walkthrough.

## Before you share the file

The file holds layout settings, but open it in a text editor and check it before you post it anywhere. Never post logs or account files publicly. If you are unsure, ask in the [FireClient Discord](https://discord.gg/r23YNWWfrx).
